analysis.one_liner: Requires airbags in all newly manufactured cars, trucks, buses, and light vehicles.
analysis.headline: The Senate passed the airbag mandate by voice vote in July 1991, but the House never voted on it, and it died when the Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required every new passenger car, truck, bus, and multipurpose passenger vehicle to come with airbags — for the driver and front passenger in cars starting September 1995, and in trucks and buses a year or two later [S3]. It treated the airbag requirement as a federal motor vehicle safety standard, enforceable under the 1966 safety law [S3]. The Senate passed it without opposition, but the House let it sit at the desk for over a year before sending it to committees, and no House vote ever happened [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Drivers and passengers in new vehicles, who would get automatic crash protection in frontal collisions without paying extra to add it themselves. Safety regulators gain an enforceable standard rather than a rule they set themselves [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Drivers and passengers in new vehicles

how_it_helps.text: All new cars manufactured on or after September 1, 1995 would have had airbags for both the driver and the front-seat passenger, with trucks, buses, and multipurpose vehicles following by September 1997 [S3].
The requirement would be legally binding as a federal motor vehicle safety standard, meaning manufacturers could be penalized for noncompliance rather than leaving airbags as an optional add-on [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Automakers, who would bear the cost of equipping every new vehicle, a cost that gets passed on to new-car buyers in the sticker price.

drawbacks.text: Equipping every vehicle with airbags adds cost to each new car, truck, and bus, which is ultimately reflected in the prices buyers pay [S3].
The bill sets fixed deadlines in statute for every vehicle category regardless of whether manufacturers are ready, leaving less room to adjust the schedule to technical or supply realities [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is a modest per-vehicle price increase for automatic crash protection on every new vehicle. The deadlines were a few years out, giving manufacturers lead time, but writing the dates into law rather than letting regulators set them is rigid by design.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate passed it by voice vote in July 1991, but it sat at the House desk for 15 months before being sent to committees in October 1992, and the Congress ended in January 1993 with no House vote ever taken.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 7, 1991 and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, which held subcommittee hearings that month and reported it favorably without amendment on June 3 [S5].
The Senate passed the bill without amendment by voice vote on July 9, 1991 [S5].
The House received the bill on July 10, 1991 and held it at the desk, with no committee referral for more than a year [S5].
On October 9, 1992 — fifteen months after Senate passage — the bill was referred jointly to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the Public Works and Transportation Committee [S5].
On December 22, 1992, less than two weeks before the 102nd Congress ended, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Transportation and Hazardous Materials, and no House vote ever occurred [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Automakers benefited, at least for the life of this bill: they avoided a statutory airbag mandate and its compliance costs because the House never acted on the Senate-passed bill.

sides.party_line_note: There was no recorded opposition: the Senate passed the bill by voice vote with bipartisan sponsorship (five cosponsors, two Republican and three Democrat), and the House never recorded any vote at all.

industries.note: The bill would have required airbags in every new light vehicle on fixed deadlines, a per-vehicle cost automakers would pass to buyers. Automakers had long argued for flexibility on airbag mandates rather than a hard statutory requirement, and the House — where they historically had their strongest defenders on safety rules — never gave the bill a vote [S3].

industries.industry: Airbag and automotive safety equipment suppliers
industries.note: A universal mandate would have created a guaranteed market for airbag systems in every new car, truck, and bus sold in the United States [S3].
